finding.origin_ip.exposed: The origin address {ip} answers in place of the {cdn} CDN (found through: {source}): the CDN protection can be bypassed
finding.origin_ip.probable: The address {ip} seems to host the site behind the {cdn} CDN (found through: {source}): to be verified
module.origin_ip.checks: Detects a CDN in front of the site, looks for the origin server address (neighbouring names, mail, SPF, DNS history) and compares the page served directly with the CDN's.
module.origin_ip.fix:
If an address is "confirmed": block right away, in the origin server's firewall and in the hosting provider's security group, the web traffic (`80`, `443`) that does not come from the address ranges published by the CDN, one rule per range, IPv4 and IPv6 (the ufw snippet shows the principle with an example range).
Better than filtering by address, which does not stop another customer of the CDN from reaching your server: authenticate the CDN to the origin. Cloudflare: Authenticated Origin Pulls (client certificate) or Cloudflare Tunnel (`cloudflared`, no inbound port at all). CloudFront: the managed prefix list `com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing` in the security group, with a secret header.
If the origin address has been known for a long time (DNS history, certificates), change it: new address or new instance, rules above applied before publishing it, then update the CDN. The old address stays in public histories: it must no longer host anything.
Remove what reveals the origin: names pointing directly to the server (`ftp`, `cpanel`, `direct`, `origin`, `dev`) to put behind the CDN or delete; e-mail sent from this same server (`MX`, SPF `ip4:`) to move to a dedicated service; test pages, headers or certificate that name the server.
Make the origin server answer without revealing anything when called by its address or by an unknown name (nginx snippet below): this hides it from a simple scan, but does not replace filtering by the CDN.
Do not count on public DNS history being erased: fix it by making the old address useless.
If the verdict is "probable" (not confirmed): test it yourself with the `curl` command in the snippet below; if the address answers with your site, apply the same steps, otherwise check that it no longer hosts anything useful.
Check from a machine outside the CDN: the `curl --resolve` request must time out or be refused; then rerun the module, which must no longer report a "confirmed" address.
module.origin_ip.title: Origin IP behind a CDN
module.origin_ip.why: If the server's real address is reachable, an attacker bypasses the CDN protection (web application firewall, rate limiting, anti-DDoS) by targeting the origin directly.
origin_ip.no_cdn: No CDN detected in front of the target: origin IP search not applicable
origin_ip.score_exposed: Origin address confirmed, reachable without going through the CDN
origin_ip.score_probable: Probable origin address, reachable without going through the CDN
